abstract: Braess's paradox -- where adding network capacity increases travel time -- is typically attributed to selfish agents. Although eusocial colonies maximize collective fitness, we find experimentally that \emph{Diacamma indicum} ants exhibit this paradox: Leaders favour the shortest path even when it slows the colony. We present a quantitative model of the exploration-exploitation trade-off, demonstrating that evolutionary forces selecting for shortest-path identification can force suboptimal global states. This proves the paradox can emerge in highly cooperative systems without individual selfishness.
